title: Spiritual Warfare
english: The law of God would not choose to do wrong, and so let us consider what it means to change the plow into a sword and the sickle into a pruning hook.

The law seems to hint to us that the time has come for those justified and sanctified in Christ to wage war against passions and sins, not to be slow in fulfilling the better things, but to transform their efforts towards virtue, and to be strong in spiritual struggles.
As the apostle Paul exhorts us, we must stand firm in truth and righteousness, and take up the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation.
The wise and gentle person is kind to divine laws.
However, there are those who pursue a life contrary to what has been said, and as a result, they are expelled from the holy multitude of saints.

God himself explains this to Moses, saying that the Israelites must send away from their camp all lepers, those with gonorrhea, and all unclean people, so they do not defile their camps where God dwells.
It would be better for God, being the ruler of holiness and justice, to show mercy to those who have suffered unfortunate events, rather than punishing them.
For leprosy, physical harm, and involuntary suffering happen to human bodies, but they are not considered sins.
No one chooses to be sick, and it is not right to punish those who are suffering.
If one of the wealthy were to choose to give up all his property to those who promise to deliver him from his suffering, it would be a preferable option.
The written law, which is meant to bring healing to the sick, would then be called into question.
The law's severity would be seen as a form of punishment, one that is perhaps too harsh for those who are already suffering.
The ways of the law are complex and multifaceted, and its desire to root out evil is uncontrolled, leading to a preference for the worse things in life.
The law's resemblance to leprosy is striking, for just as leprosy is a disease that affects the body, the law is a disease that affects the soul.
It is a corruption that spreads through the mind, leading to a defeat by excessive shame.
The law says that the one who is uncontrolled in lust is defiled, and this defilement is a passion that endures the suffering of uncontrolled lust.

The beauty of truth, on the other hand, is shown through a type and a shadow in the commandment given through Moses to the ancients, and the power of the things hidden in the mind is clearly shown in the bodily weaknesses.
The soul is afflicted with unyielding sorrow, a grief that has been taken on because of the dead and is deeply felt.
This sorrow is not something that can be easily shaken off, but rather it is a profound emotional response that has taken hold of the soul.
Those who are unable to control their passions and desires are not suited to be part of the community of the saints.
They are sent away, rejected because of their excessive contempt for the dead.
This contempt is a serious matter, one that is contrary to the will of God, who has made it clear through the words of the saints that the dead will rise again.
We are exhorted to be manly, to strive for virtue, and to be seen as better than our passions.
This is not an easy path, but rather one that requires effort and dedication.
The rewards, however, are great, for those who persevere will be able to possess the excellent achievements that come from a life of virtue.
It is pleasing to make an outline of our faith, with Jesus as the author and finisher, who endured the cross for the joy set before him, despising shame.
In what way and for what things he bore the cross for us, emptying himself, being God by nature, the Word, let us briefly elevate the narrative and apply it to the so-called voluntary emptying.
The Son, who is in him and from him by nature, is born from God and Father effortlessly and beyond mind.
The mind goes beyond bodies, and leaving behind the insignificant fantasy about them, it is better by far to think of the divine as incomparable to the nature of the body.
It is more excellent to consider it as having the glory of all that is generated and unblemished.

Let us accept, therefore, not necessarily following our own reasoning, that what is older than what is generated is that it does not exist at all; and somehow the non-existence appears before the transition into being.

title: Kenosis
english: The discussion at hand presents a clear demonstration, one that is evident and unmistakable. If the topic were about physical bodies, whether our own or others, and it were to attribute the characteristics of bodies to them, it would not be unreasonable, even if it seemed to occur naturally in the context of generated and corrupted things.

However, it is acknowledged that the path to existence is not about what does not exist at all. Instead, it will also endure the divisions that arise from the one who begets to the individualization of the one who is begotten. Furthermore, when considering the highest of all substances, the one that transcends all generated things, it is absurd to accept divisions and separations, and to seek generation in time.

The notion that the divine nature can be attributed with the properties of bodies is misguided, and it diminishes the superiority of God, which is above and beyond all created things, to a more shameful glory. The Father is always the Father, and not from the power that proceeds in time to beget, but it is necessary that the one through whom he is Father always coexists. As the Scriptures state, 'in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God' (Genesis 1:1). The concept of the 'was' is complex, and it challenges the course of thought, leading to a pursuit of understanding that is difficult to grasp.

We necessarily use the name of birth from what is ours, signifying that the Only-Begotten of the Father's substance shone forth as light by law. He subsists individually and is conceived in his own existence, and the discourse about this is entirely ineffable. For he does not exist by virtue of the begetter's substance, but rather, being himself and existing in the Father, he shows the begetter in his own nature and is worshiped and glorified together. Since he is of the same substance and equal in glory, he is necessarily co-working and equal in strength.

With the Holy Spirit subsisting together with us and being theologized and perceived together, the faith about the Holy Trinity is rightly and blamelessly conceived. The one who is well-suited to the dignities of God and the Father, through whom all things were brought forth to birth, did not consider being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but rather emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming like men (Philippians 2:7); and being found in the appearance of a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). Although he was able to revel in his own superiority and equality with the Father and to luxuriate in the riches of divinity, he willingly descended to our form, not being wronged in his own nature by the assumption of the inferior, but rather adding what was needed to himself.

It is not likely that human nature could surpass the divine and ineffable nature, and forcibly drag it to its own level. Rather, it is most dangerous to even think or say such a thing. The idea that human nature could overcome the divine nature and bring it down to its own level is not only absurd, but also harmful. On the other hand, it is wise to reason that we must yield to the nature of divinity, and allow it to surpass us. We do not say that the nature of the Word can be defined, for we claim that it cannot be defined, even if it is said to dwell in the holy body of the Virgin, but rather that it fills the heavens as God, and the earth, and the things below, and is not absent from any of the whole. And there was also a human being after this.

The divine nature is not something that can be harmed or affected by its association with human nature. Just as the sun's light is not harmed by shining on the mire and marshes, the divine nature remains unharmed and unchanged. Those who think that they can share in the divine glory and define the unseemly as part of the best economy are mistaken. They do not accept the mystery of the divine nature, and are instead puffed up with pride and haughtiness.

Those who laugh at our beliefs think that the matter is foolish and that we are compared to lifeless objects. They do not understand that their own teachers, if they had grasped something to think or say, would have difficulty in keeping the faith and the saying 'He himself said', and then they would have opposed their own thoughts to the divine judgments, pouring them into their own heads with great difficulty. They do not honor these things with the divine nature, but rather think that someone has thoroughly investigated the matter. For they ask how the undefiled mind, which is free from quantity and definition, can be enclosed in a human body.

It is said that it is a small thing for the God who is above all to become like us. However, you accuse Him because, being philanthropic and good by nature, He has taken more care for us than is fitting. This is acknowledged to be a small thing for Him, which is called kenosis. Nevertheless, the word of His gentleness towards us will be shown to be consistent with Scripture. What is truly worthy of wonder is that He has taken on the causes of our salvation. One might ask how He has done this without being impious. Tell me, then, whether you think it would have been better for Him to leave us bound by our sins, or rather to save us and show us care. How can one doubt that it is fitting for the good God to distribute goods to those who have come from Him?

We will allow doctors to deal with the treatment of passions, but we will rebuke God for not being ignorant of the way of our care. For it would be absurd to think that God, who is above all, would not know the way of our care, and would not take care of us in a way that is fitting for Him.
